excerpt: How to open WhatsApp on a laptop with the keyboard, what stays on the computer afterwards, and how to sign out of a machine you do not own.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to use WhatsApp on a computer. You will open it with a QR code, type with a keyboard, send a document, and sign out properly when you finish. If your phone keyboard makes long messages painful, this is the fix.
WhatsApp Web is not a second account. It is a window into the chat already on your phone, which means the phone must stay connected and switched on for it to work.
Before you start

items: A phone with WhatsApp and an internet connection.
A computer with a browser.
Your phone beside you, because the sign-in happens there.

body.text: Open it with the QR code

items: On the computer, open a browser and type web.whatsapp.com in the address bar.
A square code appears on the screen.
On the phone, open WhatsApp, then Settings, then Linked devices.
Choose Link a device, and point the phone camera at the square.
The chats load on the computer within a few seconds.

body.text: You will see your chat list fill in on the left of the screen, and a small note at the bottom of the phone app saying it is linked. The phone can stay in your pocket, as long as it has data and a battery.

body.alt: A laptop screen showing WhatsApp Web with a chat list.
body.caption: WhatsApp Web mirrors the phone. The phone stays the account, and the computer is only a window.

body.text: It looks like the computer has its own WhatsApp account. It does not, and if the phone is off or offline, the computer stops receiving messages too.
Type, send, and attach
The reason to use a computer is the keyboard and the larger screen. Long messages, documents, and careful replies are all easier here.

items: Click a chat on the left to open it.
Type in the box at the bottom and press Enter to send.
Press Shift and Enter for a new line without sending.
Click the paperclip to send a document, a photograph, or a picture from the computer.
Rename the file before you send it, so the reader can tell what it is.
Search a chat with the search box at the top, which finds text you sent months ago.

body.text: None of this needs a new account, and the messages stay on the phone as well. That is why a chat you send from the laptop is still there when you pick up the phone.

body.alt: A phone beside a laptop both showing the same chat.
body.caption: One conversation, two screens. Send from the laptop and it appears on the phone at the same moment.

body.text: Sign out of a machine that is not yours
A linked device stays linked until you remove it. On a business centre computer, that means the next customer can read your chats.

items: On the computer, click the menu at the top left and choose Log out.
Or on the phone, open Linked devices and remove that computer.
Do both if you are unsure, because removal from the phone works even when the computer is switched off.
Check the linked devices list once a month for anything you do not recognise.
Never link a device on a machine you do not control for longer than the session.

body.text: Do not worry if you forget once. Removing the device from the phone ends the session on the computer within a minute.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a fix that takes under a minute, and none of them needs support.

items: The QR code will not scan: clean the phone lens, and hold it steady at the right distance.
The computer shows Connecting and nothing loads: check the phone is online and awake.
Messages stop arriving on the computer: the phone lost connection. Reconnect it, then refresh the page.
A document will not send: it is too large. Reduce or zip it, or send a link.
The computer signed itself out: the session expired. Link it again with the phone.
You left it linked on a public computer: open Linked devices on the phone and remove it now.

body.text: Practice
Do this once on your own laptop, and once on a borrowed one to feel the difference.

items: Link WhatsApp Web on your own computer.
Send yourself a document from the computer.
Search a chat for a word you used last month.
Open Linked devices on the phone and look at the list.
Log out on the computer, and confirm the phone says it is unlinked.

body.text: You can now type long messages and send documents without fighting a phone keyboard. In the next lesson you will use maps to reach a place you have never been.

excerpt: How to search for a place, read a route before you leave, share your location with somebody waiting for you, and what to do when the map loses you.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to use a map on a phone to reach a place you have never visited. You will search for the address, read the route before you leave, share your location with somebody waiting, and recover when the map loses you. It works with data, and partly without it.

A map app is a moving picture of streets with a blue dot for you. The dot comes from satellites and from phone masts, and it is usually accurate to a few metres, which is enough to tell which side of a road you are on.
You will see the map open centred on your position, with the search box at the top and a blue dot that pulses when it is unsure of where you are.
Before you start

items: A phone with Google Maps or a similar app.
Location turned on for the app.
Enough data for the trip, or a downloaded offline map.

body.text: Search, then read the route

items: Open the maps app and type the place name or address in the search box.
Tap the result that matches the town or the area you expect.
Tap Directions, then choose walking, driving, or public transport.
Read the whole route once before you start moving.
Check the travel time, then add half of it again for real traffic.
Tap Start so that the map follows you and speaks the turns.

body.text: You will see the route drawn as a thick line with a blue dot at your position, and a bar at the top showing the next turn and the distance to it. When the bar changes while you walk, the map is keeping up with you.

body.alt: A phone showing a map route with a blue location dot.
body.caption: Read the whole route before you move. The bar at the top tells you the next turn, so you do not have to stare at the screen.

body.text: It looks like the map knows the place exactly. Many Nigerian addresses are described by landmarks rather than street numbers, so search for the landmark and check the pin is where you expect before you travel.
Let somebody know where you are
Sharing your location is useful when you are meeting somebody, and it is a sensible precaution when you are going somewhere unfamiliar.

items: Tap the blue dot and choose Share location.
Choose a contact, and set the duration rather than sharing indefinitely.
Send a screenshot of the route as a second option.
For a delivery, send a pin instead of a long description.
Stop sharing when you arrive, so the other person is not tracking you for days.

body.text: None of this costs money beyond data, and the timer means you do not have to remember to switch it off.

body.alt: A person using a phone map while walking outside.
body.caption: A shared pin ends more arguments than a written description. Send the pin, and stop sharing when you arrive.

body.text: When the map loses you
Maps fail in a few ordinary ways: weak signal, a wrong turn, or a place that does not exist on the map. Each has a next step that costs nothing.

items: The dot drifts or spins: step outside, wait twenty seconds, and let the phone find the satellites.
The route recalculates constantly: the app is fighting a wrong position. Stop, confirm where you are on the map, then start again.
You missed the turn: the app recalculates by itself, and there is no need to turn around on a busy road.
You have no data: download the map of your area before you travel, then the route works offline.
The place is not on the map: use a landmark, and ask a person nearby rather than circling.
The battery is low: turn off the spoken directions, lower the brightness, and let the phone rest between checks.

body.text: Do not worry about the map being wrong in some areas. It is a guide, and the person at the junction usually knows the last hundred metres better than the satellite.
If it goes wrong
These six cases cover most trips that go wrong, and each one has a practical answer.

items: The app will not open: check data, then location permission, then restart the phone.
The map shows the wrong town: the search matched a similarly named place. Add the state to the search.
The route sends you into a closed road: tap the route options and choose another, or follow the diversion and let it recalculate.
The voice directions are silent: raise the media volume, which is separate from the ring volume.
You cannot find the exact building: use street view or satellite view to recognise the entrance.
You are running late: share your location and an honest time, which is more useful than three apologies.

body.text: Practice
One real journey planned properly teaches more than a page about it.

items: Search for a place you know well, and check the pin is in the right spot.
Plan a route to it and read the whole thing before starting.
Share your location with one person for fifteen minutes.
Download the offline map for your area.
Stop sharing and confirm the other person can no longer see you.

body.text: You can now travel to an unfamiliar place without depending on a description. In the next lesson you will make a poster that somebody can actually read from across a room.

excerpt: How to make a poster that reads from a distance: one message, big type, one image, and a phone number people can see. Made in Word or Canva, printed at a business centre.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to make a poster that people can read from across a room. You will choose one message, set type big enough to see, add one image, and print it at a business centre. No design software experience is needed.

A poster has roughly three seconds to be understood by somebody walking past. That means one message, large text, and a clear way to contact you. Everything else is decoration that competes with the message.
You will see the finished page at the size it will print, and it looks odd on a bright screen because large type is meant to be read from far away.
If you have never made one before, that is fine. A heading, a picture, and a phone number are the whole poster, and Word can make all three.
Before you start

items: Word, Canva, or any program that can make a page.
One photograph or logo you have the right to use.
A phone number or address you can print in large type.

body.text: Decide the one thing
Write the sentence you want a stranger to remember, in ten words or fewer. If you cannot, the poster is trying to do two jobs.
It looks like a poster needs a designer. A stranger walking past reads the biggest words first, and that is a decision you make in one minute.

items: Write the message first, in a sentence: Computer classes start Monday.
Cut it to the shortest version that still tells the truth.
Decide the one action: call, come to the address, or scan a code.
Choose the audience, because a poster for students differs from one for shop owners.
Put the price or the words Free only if you mean it.

body.text: You will see the message look too plain on screen at this stage. That is normal, because a poster is read at a distance and the size does the work.

body.alt: A simple poster with large heading text and one image.
body.caption: One message, one image, one phone number. Everything else is optional, and most of it is noise.

body.text: Set it up so it reads

items: Choose A4 for a noticeboard, or A3 for a wall.
Use one font family. Two at most, one for the heading and one for the details.
Make the heading large enough to read at three metres, which is about 60 point on A4.
Keep the details at about 24 point or larger.
Leave a margin around the edge of at least one centimetre.
Put the phone number at the bottom, in the same place every time.

body.text: None of this needs a design app. Word will do it, and a business centre can print A3 for a few hundred naira.

body.alt: A printed poster pinned to a noticeboard.
body.caption: Print one copy and look at it from three metres before you print twenty.

body.text: Print, then check it on the wall
A poster looks different on paper and at a distance. One test print prevents twenty expensive mistakes.

items: Print one copy at the business centre before ordering more.
Pin it up and walk three metres away.
Read the heading first, then the phone number. If either needs effort, enlarge it.
Check that the photograph is sharp, not stretched.
Ask one person what the poster is advertising, without helping them.

body.text: Do not worry about filling every space. Empty space is what makes large text readable, and a crowded poster is the most common beginner mistake.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is fixable in the file before you print, which is the cheapest place to fix it.

items: The text is cut off at the edge: the printer has an unprintable margin. Move everything inward.
The photograph is blurry: it was small and you enlarged it. Use a larger image or remove it.
The colours print differently: screens and printers differ. Choose strong contrasting colours rather than pale ones.
The font changed on the print shop's computer: save as a PDF before you go.
Nobody can read the phone number: make it the largest line after the heading.
The poster looks busy: remove one element. Then remove one more.

body.text: Practice
One real poster, printed once, checked from three metres away.

items: Write your message in ten words or fewer.
Lay it out on A4 with one heading, one image, and one phone number.
Save it as a PDF so the layout cannot move.
Print one copy and read it from three metres.
Ask somebody what it advertises, then adjust once and print again.

body.text: You can now make a poster that works in a hallway rather than only on your screen. In the next lesson you will shrink a photograph so that email will accept it.

excerpt: Why a phone photo is too big to send, how to make it small enough without ruining it, and the settings that matter for a form or a passport picture.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to make a photograph small enough to email or upload, without turning it into a blur. You will check the file size, reduce it, and know the settings that matter for forms and passport photographs.

A photograph from a phone camera is large because it holds millions of tiny dots. Most forms want fewer dots, and most inboxes refuse anything over about 25 MB. Reducing the size changes how many dots are kept, not what the picture shows.
It looks like a large file must be a better photograph. The size mostly comes from the number of pixels, and a form that asks for a small file is asking for fewer of them.
Before you start

items: One photograph from your phone, already on the computer.
The size limit the form or the inbox asks for, if there is one.
About ten minutes.

body.text: Check the size first
You cannot fix a size you have not read. One right-click answers the question.

items: Right-click the file and choose Properties.
Read the size in MB, and the dimensions in pixels.
Compare it with the limit you were given.
If it is under the limit, stop. There is nothing to fix.
If it is over, decide whether to reduce the dimensions or the quality.

body.text: You will see the dimensions written as two numbers, such as 4000 by 3000. Those are the dots across and down, and halving them cuts the file to about a quarter of its size.

body.alt: A file properties window showing an image size in megabytes.
body.caption: Properties tells you the size and the dimensions. Most photographs need one reduction, not five.

body.text: It looks as a smallerer file must be a worse picture. A photograph reduced from 4000 pixels to 1600 looks the same on a phone screen and prints acceptably at A5, which is what most forms need.
Reduce it in three ways
Use whichever tool you already have. All three produce a file the other person can open.

items: On Windows, open the photo in Paint, choose Resize, and set a percentage such as 40 percent, then Save As.
In Photos on Windows, choose the three dots, then Resize, and pick a size.
On a phone, use the share menu and choose a smaller size when the app offers it.
Online compressors work, but only use one you trust with the picture.
For a form, follow its stated pixel size exactly rather than guessing.

body.text: None of this changes the original if you use Save As with a new name. Keep the original, and send the small copy.

body.alt: A photo editor showing a resize dialog with a percentage field.
body.caption: Resize by percentage and save under a new name. The original stays full size for printing later.

body.text: What forms and passport pictures want
Official forms have specific rules, and meeting them prevents a rejection that takes a week to reverse.

items: Read the limits: usually a maximum in pixels and a maximum in kilobytes.
Use a plain background for a passport photograph, not a patterned wall.
Keep the whole head and the top of the shoulders in the frame.
Save as JPG for photographs, and PNG only for images with text.
Name the file with your name and what it is: ada-okoro-passport.jpg.
Keep the full-size original, because a printed version needs more detail.

body.text: Do not worry if the first attempt is rejected for size. Change one number, save a new copy, and try again. The step that matters is reading the exact limit.
If it goes wrong
These six problems cover most upload and attachment failures.

items: The file is still too large: reduce the dimensions rather than the quality alone.
The picture is now blurry: you reduced too far. Go back to the original and stop at a larger size.
The form rejects the type: it wants JPG, and you saved PNG.
The form rejects the dimensions: set exactly the pixels it asks for.
The colours look wrong: the file was saved in an unusual profile. Save again as standard JPG.
The photograph is sideways: rotate it in the viewer and save, then upload again.

body.text: Practice
One photograph, reduced once, checked in the email that sends it.

items: Read the size and dimensions of one phone photograph.
Reduce it to about 40 percent and save under a new name.
Compare the two files on screen at full size.
Attach the smaller one to an email and confirm it sends.
Write down the settings that worked, for the next form.

body.text: You can now send a photograph that arrives, opens, and is accepted. In the next lesson you will deal with the message that says your computer has a virus.

excerpt: Why most virus warnings are adverts, how to tell a real infection from a fake alarm, what a scan actually does, and what to do if the warning is genuine.

body.text: This lesson explains what the phrase your computer has a virus usually means. Most warnings are adverts pretending to be security software, and a few are genuine. You will learn how to tell them apart, how to close a fake alarm safely, and what a real scan does.

A virus is a program that copies itself or damages files without permission. An advert is a page designed to look like a virus warning so that you buy something or call a number. The two look similar on purpose, and the difference is where the message appears.
Before you start

items: The computer with the warning on it.
A phone, in case you need to search for the exact words.
About fifteen minutes.

body.text: Where the message appears tells you what it is
Real security software uses the operating system's own notification. Fake alarms live inside a browser page, and they stop when the page closes.

items: A box in the corner of the screen from Windows Security is likely genuine.
A full-page red warning with a phone number and a countdown is an advert.
A warning that appears while browsing, in a tab, is almost always fake.
A voice reading the warning aloud is always fake, and it is done to alarm you.
A message telling you not to close the window is fake, because a browser can always be closed.

body.text: You will see the fake warning use a real company's name and logo, and sometimes a list of scary file names. None of it is evidence, because a logo takes a minute to copy.

body.alt: A browser page showing a fake virus warning with a phone number.
body.caption: A phone number and a countdown in the alarm are the marks of an advert. Real security software never asks you to call.

body.text: It looks like closing the window will make it worse. Closing a tab has never damaged a computer, and it is the correct first move.
Close it safely

items: Press Alt and F4 to close the window, or Ctrl and W to close the tab.
If the pop-up will not close, press Ctrl, Shift and Escape, then end the browser in Task Manager.
Do not click anywhere inside the warning, including a Close button on the page itself.
Do not call any number shown, whoever answers.
Clear the browser history and cookies for that site, then reopen the browser normally.
If it returns on every start, check the browser extensions and remove anything you did not add.

body.text: None of this deletes your files, and the browser comes back exactly as it was apart from the site that produced the alarm.

body.alt: A hand pressing Alt and F4 to close a browser window.
body.caption: Alt and F4 closes the window. Never use a Close button drawn inside the fake warning.

body.text: What a real scan does
If you want to know whether the machine is actually infected, run the protection that came with it. That is the only answer worth trusting.

items: Open Windows Security from the Start menu, or Security and Privacy on a Mac.
Choose Virus and threat protection, then Quick scan.
Wait for it to finish, and read the result rather than the progress bar.
Turn on real-time protection if it is off.
Keep one protection tool only. Two antivirus programs fight each other.
Update the definitions, since an old scanner misses new threats.

body.text: Do not worry about the scan taking an hour. A quick scan covers the places infections usually hide, and a full scan is for a machine that is already behaving oddly.
If the warning is genuine
Sometimes the machine really is infected. The signs are slow behaviour, pop-ups at start-up, a browser homepage that changed by itself, or files that will not open.

items: Disconnect from the internet, so the program cannot send anything out.
Run a full scan with the protection you already have.
Remove what it finds, and follow the restart it asks for.
Change the passwords for email and banking from another device.
Back up your documents before taking the machine for repair.
If it will not clean, ask a repairer to reinstall the system, and restore only your own documents.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here has a safe next step, and the first two are the ones people get wrong.

items: The warning will not close: end the browser in Task Manager, then reopen it.
The page reappears on every start: remove the extension, and reset the browser settings.
The browser homepage changed: set it back in Settings, and remove the tool that changed it.
You paid for a fake cleaner: call your bank and block the card, then change the password on that site.
You called the number and let them in: disconnect, change your passwords from another device, and run a full scan.
A scan finds nothing but the machine is still odd: update the system, check the storage, and test with another user account.

body.text: Practice
Ten minutes with the real security screen, so the fake one never surprises you.

items: Open Windows Security and read the current status.
Run a quick scan and note how long it takes.
Look at the browser extensions list and remove one you do not use.
Practise closing a window with Alt and F4.
Write down the exact wording of the next fake warning you see, and notice it does not match the real screen.

body.text: You can now tell an advert from an infection, which is the whole skill. In the next lesson the chapter turns to the quieter kind of danger, the message that copies a familiar voice.
